text: A Group Policy Object does nothing on its own — it only takes effect once it's linked to a site, a domain, or an OU, and Windows applies every linked GPO in a fixed order. This lesson walks through that order, what happens when two linked GPOs disagree about the same setting, and the two command-line tools you use to prove what actually took effect on a real machine instead of just hoping it did.

GPOs apply in LSDOU order — Local policy first, then Site, then Domain, then OU, with a parent OU applying before its child OU. When two linked GPOs touch the same setting, the one applied later wins, so an OU-linked GPO overrides a domain-linked GPO by default. gpupdate /force pushes an immediate policy refresh instead of waiting for the normal 90-minute cycle, and gpresult /r shows the Resultant Set of Policy — exactly which GPOs applied and which got filtered out.

Take a domain-level GPO setting minimum password length to 8, and a Finance OU GPO setting it to 14. Because OU-linked GPOs apply after domain-linked ones in LSDOU order, Finance users end up needing 14-character passwords while everyone else only needs 8 — not a misconfiguration, just inheritance doing exactly what it's designed to do.

Block Inheritance, set on an OU, stops ordinary site- and domain-linked GPOs from reaching it. Enforced, set on a specific GPO at a higher level, overrides that block outright — it's a property of the GPO being pushed down, not something the receiving OU can opt out of. A domain-wide password-compliance GPO set to Enforced still reaches an OU that's blocking inheritance for everything else.

Confirm what actually applied with gpupdate /force to refresh immediately, then gpresult /r to see the Resultant Set of Policy. Next: before configuring any of this by hand, Lesson 6 covers security baselines and the CIS Benchmarks — the tested starting points real organizations build from instead of guessing at every setting.
